summary: BGP session from R1 to 10.255.0.2 went down, with 11 related findings on R1, R2, R3, R4. Severity is critical: the most serious finding is "BGP session from R1 to 10.255.0.2 went down". The likely root cause: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on R1 was down for 8m 36s (the tool's confidence is high: every finding is accounted for, the timing matches how the protocols behave, and 4 devices report it). An interface that goes down and stays down is most often a cable, an optic, or the device at the other end being off. An interface is a port on the device; its optic is the plug-in module that turns electrical signals into light for a fiber cable. BGP is the protocol routers use to exchange routes with other networks, over a long-lived session with each neighbor; the hold timer is how long a router waits without hearing from a neighbor before it closes the session. OSPF is the protocol routers use to learn routes inside one network; an adjacency is the working relationship between two OSPF neighbors, kept alive by hello messages, and the dead timer is how long a router waits without a hello before giving up.

hypotheses.text: The likely root cause: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on R1 was down for 8m 36s. It accounts for 12 of the incident's 12 findings. The tool's confidence is high: every finding is accounted for, the timing matches how the protocols behave, and 4 devices report it.

impact.text: Everything that used this interface lost its path until the interface came back.
OSPF runs over that interface, so the router dropped its neighbors there the moment the interface went down.
BGP between loopback addresses depends on OSPF for the route to its peer; once the OSPF adjacency was lost the BGP session timed out.
BGP keepalives from the device whose interface failed stopped arriving, so its peers closed their sessions when the hold timer ran out.
The other routers stopped hearing OSPF hellos from the device whose interface failed, and gave up on it when the 40-second dead timer ran out.

fix_steps.text: Look at the status and the error counters of GigabitEthernet0/1 on R1. A healthy interface is up with counters that stay still; rising input or CRC errors mean a bad signal is arriving.

Inspect the cable and the optic at both ends, and confirm that the device at the other end is powered and its port is not shut. A link needs both ends and the cable between them, and the logs come from one end only.

If the port is in the err-disabled state, find out why before bringing it back. Err-disabled means the switch turned the port off to protect itself, and it will do so again until the reason is removed.
Shut and no shut the interface only after the physical checks, and only if it is still down. This restarts the port, which interrupts anything still using it.

verification_commands.purpose: The interface and the line protocol are both up, and the input error and CRC counters are not rising.

unknowns: Why the interface went down. The logs show that it did, not whether a cable, an optic or the device at the other end was at fault.
Neighbor addresses not matched to a device in these logs: 10.255.0.2, 10.255.0.3, 10.255.0.4. List them in a topology file to say which device each one is.
